Un cimetière musulman à Québec pour vivr: A Muslim cemetery in Quebec City to live and die in peace
Après l’ouverture, plusieurs décès ont f: After it opened, several deaths struck Quebec City’s Muslim community.
Quatre ans après les attentats à la gran: Four years after the attack on Quebec City’s Grand Mosque, the Muslim Quebecers of the Old Capital finally got their Muslim cemetery, far from the spotlight. After more than 22 years of waiting, the long-hoped-for cemetery opened on June 11, 2020.
« Toute la communauté musulmane de Québe: “The whole Muslim community in Quebec City knows the cemetery exists, and the whole city of Quebec knows it too. What we avoided was the press, because a cemetery isn’t something you just publicize like that. It’s done with simplicity,” Boufeldja Benabdallah, president of the Centre culturel islamique de Québec (CCIQ) and co-founder of the cemetery, tells us.
Sur les lieux, près de l’autoroute à Sai: On site, near the highway in Sainte-Foy, he says a prayer in front of the modest snow-covered graves, marked with numbers engraved on small green plaques. “This summer, we’ll be adding headstones and trees,” he says at the entrance to the cemetery, which is enclosed by a green fence.
Cela fait plus de sept mois que le cimet: The Muslim cemetery of Quebec City quietly opened its doors more than seven months ago. Yet its construction was a source of division, particularly after the attack on the Quebec City mosque.
En témoignent les réactions au projet de: Just look at the reactions to the cemetery project that was initially supposed to be built in Saint-Apollinaire. On July 16, 2017, residents rejected it in a referendum. That was followed by a string of hateful acts against the CCIQ, including <l1>a car being set on fire</l1> and <l2>packages</l2> containing racist messages being sent.
Un peu moins de six mois auparavant, le: A little less than six months earlier, on January 29, 2017, the terrorist had walked into the Centre culturel islamique de Québec and murdered six men, and wounded eight others. That Sunday, Ibrahima Barry, Mamadou Tanou Barry, Khaled Belkacemi, Aboubaker Thabti, Abdelkrim Hassane and Azzedine Soufiane never came home after evening prayer. That Sunday, they fell to the bullets of hatred.
Tristement, l’attentat perpétré au CCIQ: Sadly, the attack at the CCIQ was a trigger. “We realized there was no place where the victims could be laid to rest,” says Nader, a young Muslim civil servant who preferred not to give his last name. All the families had to have the bodies repatriated, except for one of the deceased, who was transferred to Montréal’s Muslim cemetery, located in Laval.
À l’époque, l’idée d’un cimetière n’étai: At the time, the idea of a cemetery wasn’t new, but the tragic circumstances of the attack revealed its necessity to the province. More than three years later, when the cemetery finally opened, the community didn’t want to draw attention. It was a time for restraint, contemplation and spirituality.
« Dès le premier jour, on a enterré deux: “On the very first day, we buried two men. Their last wish was to be laid to rest in the city where they had lived, raised their children and grown old. They were worshippers at the Grand Mosque,” says the cemetery’s co-founder.
Le premier a perdu la vie à 60 ans, un m: The first died at 60, a month and a half before the cemetery opened. His last wish was to be buried there. Temporarily buried on the grounds of a funeral home, he was transferred a month and a half later, becoming the first believer buried in the Muslim cemetery of Quebec City. The other was a close friend of Boufeldja’s, “like a brother.” He was 80 and died two days before the inauguration. “So on opening day, we ended up with two burials. We brought both of them, but the first one, who had made the wish to his family, was laid in the grave one minute before the other.”
Depuis, neuf adultes et quatre bébés ont: Since then, nine adults and four babies have been buried there.
Après l’ouverture, plusieurs décès ont f: After it opened, several deaths struck Quebec City’s Muslim community. What mattered most was meeting the needs of people who wanted to be buried in Quebec City, says Jihad*, who prefers not to give her last name.
« Il y avait une volonté de vivre ça ent: “There was a desire to experience this among ourselves, to keep it private. Death is very intimate in itself. And for Muslims, it’s also something we’re very modest about,” adds the 28-year-old self-employed worker.
« Pour nous, la mort est une demeure éte: “For us, death is an eternal dwelling. Everybody thinks about the house they live in. Well, we also think about our eternal home. That’s why it’s important,” explains Jihad, who feels there was needless hostility toward a request that was “so simple.” For the young woman, having a place where her loved ones can rest in peace is essential. She thinks it’s “crazy” that such a simple request not only took so long, but also caused such a fuss.
« La génération de mes parents est venue: “My parents’ generation came here for a better life, not to convert everybody! Taking care of yourself and your community is already a lot of work,” Jihad says wryly of the accusations of proselytizing aimed at Quebec’s Muslims. “We’ve wanted this cemetery to open forever,” she says.

Les démarches pour construire ce cimetiè: The process to build this cemetery began in 1998, Mr. Benabdallah tells us. Why did it take so long? Beyond public mistrust, lengthy administrative procedures explain the delays, particularly regarding the land, the cemetery’s co-founder believes. “We started submitting applications, but we kept running into the zoning issue,” he recounts.
Tout projet de cimetière implique en eff: Any cemetery project does indeed involve several administrative steps. Large sums of money must also be raised during the process, which requires rigour and bureaucratic know-how.
Un autre élément est en outre venu compl: Another factor further complicated matters: the land had to belong to the community in perpetuity. “In our religion, the ground where someone is buried belongs to them until the end of time,” explains Mr. Benabdallah.
C’est la raison pour laquelle il souhait: That’s why he was determined to buy a piece of land rather than depend on a funeral company, which could have resold it.

C’est après l’attentat, en 2017, que ce: It was after the attack, in 2017, that this long process picked up speed. “It accelerated [its] creation. In this great tragedy, there was an understanding [of our situation],” says Mr. Benabdallah.
Ainsi, Régis Labeaume, le maire de Québe: Quebec City mayor Régis Labeaume ultimately decided to use his influence to help the community after the attack. Discreetly, he mobilized his staff to find a piece of municipal land at cost. His goal was to avoid fuelling controversy and debate.
Nous avons communiqué avec le bureau du: We contacted the Quebec City mayor’s office for Mr. Labeaume’s comments, but he is not giving any interviews until February 8. In December 2017, when the land was sold, he<l1> spoke</l1> about the matter: “I deliberately moved quickly because I didn’t want us to have a debate about it.”
Avant le 11 juin 2020, les musulmans de: Before June 11, 2020, Muslims in Quebec City and its surrounding area had no place to bury their dead. “Not being able to bury them here was an added headache,” says Nader. The young man now lives in Ottawa, but he grew up in Quebec City, where his family still lives.
Avant l’ouverture du cimetière de Québec: Before the Quebec City cemetery opened, a deceased person’s family had several options: send the body abroad for the modest sum of $15,000 to $20,000, transport it to Montréal to be buried in the only Muslim cemetery in Quebec, or bury it in a Catholic cemetery and see Muslim rites adapted to Catholic tradition. Beyond the adjustments they involve, these options are costly. Transporting a body can be problematic for several reasons.
D’abord, certains ménages modestes ne di: First, some low-income households don’t have the money needed and have to turn to relatives or the community to cover it, with some even launching crowdfunding campaigns. Second, according to Muslim rites, the body must be buried as quickly as possible. “In Islam, it’s good to be buried where you die. Nearly 90% of people are buried in Quebec,” explains Jihad.
Depuis l’inauguration du cimetière de Qu: Since the Quebec City cemetery was inaugurated, the city’s Muslims can bury their dead in a way that is as close as possible to their traditions, but also near family and loved ones. “If a member of my family were buried in my country of origin, Lebanon, I couldn’t visit the grave regularly. I wouldn’t grieve the same way.
On veut pouvoir enterrer nos morts à côt: We want to be able to bury our dead near where we live,” Nader sums up. The fact that his parents are getting older is forcing the family to think about their deaths, and therefore where they will be buried. For him, it’s logical and natural that they be buried in Quebec City. “Living most of your life in one place and not being able to be buried there is strange,” he says.
Plus qu’un lieu de vie éternelle, ce cim: More than a place of eternal life, this cemetery thus represents the culmination of a quest, a symbol of integration. “I’m happy we’ve closed the loop. Because we are full-fledged citizens. We are Muslim Quebecers. We love Quebec so much that we want to be buried here!” Boufeldja Benabdallah exclaims fervently.
« Pour certains, c’était une consécratio: “For some, it was a crowning achievement. We are truly part of the fabric of Quebec City,” says Nader, who is nonetheless more critical about the cemetery’s approval. For him, as for others, the cemetery is only one step toward equality, and the same problems of racism and Islamophobia persist in Quebec.
« La tragédie de 2017 n’est pas sortie d: “The 2017 tragedy didn’t come out of nowhere. There’s a context that explains what happened. The climate of hatred is still there. When you walk around Quebec City, and even elsewhere, the worry remains,” Nader laments. The insults shouted in the streets are too many to count, along with the veils ripped off, the curious or inappropriate remarks, well-meaning or not, the prejudice and the discrimination.
« L’histoire du cimetière musulman de Qu: “The story of the Muslim cemetery of Quebec City is a striking example of systemic racism,” the young man asserts. Like him, many denounce the 22-year obstacle course they had to endure for a very simple request.
« Vivre dans la tranquillité, c’est tout: “Living in peace is all the community has asked for since it’s existed,” Nader says. Living and dying in peace, plain and simple.

Selon Statistique Canada, 300 000 citoye: According to Statistics Canada, 300,000 Muslims live in Quebec. The Muslim cemetery of Quebec City can hold 850 burials. At the Hamza Muslim cemetery in Laval, nearly 500 plots are occupied and nearly 3,500 are vacant. At the Laval cemetery, the Muslim section has 400 plots in development and 300 occupied. A few other sections exist within Catholic and multi-faith cemeteries, but these are not suited to all Muslim burial rites. In Sherbrooke, if a Muslim cemetery project comes to fruition, nearly 400 people could be buried there.
À Sherbrooke, on attend aussi un cimetiè: In Sherbrooke, people have also been waiting for a Muslim cemetery for more than 20 years. The deed of sale for the land was signed in November 2020. Nearly $120,000 still needs to be raised to complete work before the cemetery can open. “It’s not an accessible process. It requires a lot of resources and expertise that our community didn’t have,” explains Mohamed Golli, spokesperson for the Association culturelle islamique de l’Estrie (ACIE), which is in charge of the project.
<l1>L’Association de la sépulture musulm: <l1>The Association de la sépulture musulmane au Québec</l1> can be a valuable source of help for grieving families. It offers assistance with arrangements and administrative procedures, as well as with raising the funds needed to cover the costs.
